name: Neurocardiogenic Syncope

prevalence.estimate: Up to 40% of population experiences at least one episode

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: European Society of Cardiology 2018 Guidelines for Syncope

criteria.description: Transient loss of consciousness with rapid onset, short duration, and spontaneous complete recovery
Triggered by prolonged standing, emotional stress, pain, or heat exposure
Associated prodromal symptoms: lightheadedness, warmth, diaphoresis, nausea, pallor, visual dimming
Positive head-up tilt table test reproducing symptoms with hypotension and/or bradycardia
Absence of structural heart disease or other causes of syncope on initial evaluation

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Clinical history consistent with reflex syncope with identifiable trigger and prodrome; tilt table test supportive but not required
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Often a clinical diagnosis based on history. Tilt table testing has moderate sensitivity (~60-70%) and specificity.

pathognomonic.symptomName: Transient loss of consciousness preceded by prodrome and triggered by orthostatic stress or vagal stimulus
pathognomonic.notes: The hallmark presentation; loss of consciousness is brief (seconds to <1 min)
searchTerms: fainting with warning signs triggered by standing
passing out after feeling dizzy when standing
brief loss of consciousness with prodrome and triggers
temporary loss of brightness in sight

occasional.notes: Can mimic epileptic seizure; convulsive syncope

searchTerms: loss of bladder control during episode
heart stops beating for over 3 seconds

other: Positive head-up tilt table test (hypotension ± bradycardia with symptom reproduction)
Implantable loop recorder may document asystole in recurrent cases

distinguishingFeatures: POTS features chronic orthostatic tachycardia without frank syncope in most cases
NCS is episodic with hypotension/bradycardia at the time of LOC
Neurogenic OH has sustained BP drop on standing without the reflex bradycardia
NCS is paroxysmal with identifiable triggers
Arrhythmic syncope typically has abrupt onset without prodrome
May have abnormal ECG at baseline

redFlags: Family history of sudden cardiac death
No prodromal symptoms before loss of consciousness
New onset in older adults (>60) without prior history
references: Brignole M, et al. 2018 ESC Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of syncope. Eur Heart J. 2018;39(21):1883-1948.
